title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered power target sought a 5 percentage‑point minimum detectable effect; given the observed near‑ceiling baseline the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains. Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we report artifacts, analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar for binary outcomes), and detailed execution accounting to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on surrounding orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on an LLM alone [1,2]. A canonical mitigation strategy is the generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architecture: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules [3–5].

Despite conceptual support for verifier scaffolding, there is comparatively little preregistered, traceable, paired evidence quantifying whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement—defined here as a rollback‑aware binary episode success—over a one‑shot generation approach. We designed NetOpsTraceBench to fill that gap with a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded experiment that isolates guard value while holding the shared initial LLM candidate constant. Our central research question, posed before execution, was: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topology clusters (edge vs core)?

Contributions. (1) A preregistered experimental design and frozen analysis plan (study ID rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712). (2) A paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic validator, and Mininet‑style emulation with full execution accounting. (3) Transparent reporting of analytic deviation (Wilcoxon ↦ exact McNemar for paired binary outcomes), complete failure/missingness accounting, and representative artifact‑grounded diagnostics (provider audit, validator traces, task manifests) that explain why the guarded pipeline rarely required repair under our design.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and recent system papers position LLMs within AIOps/NetOps pipelines and repeatedly call for workflow‑centered evaluation that includes verifier steps, provenance, and execution‑ground outcomes rather than solely QA metrics [1,6]. Work on verifier‑guided NL→formal translations (e.g., CTL/NuSMV workflows) and intent→topology compilation demonstrates the feasibility of generate–validate‑repair approaches in constrained domains [3,7]. Prototype systems for text→config (PreConfig, TopoIntent) and LLM‑assisted misconfiguration detection (GenKubeSec) further show domain viability but typically evaluate on constructed or small held‑out sets [4,5,11].

Empirical studies and position pieces document LLM failure modes relevant to NetOps—hallucination, semantic/unit errors, overconfidence/miscalibration, prompt‑injection vulnerability, and provenance loss—which motivate guarded architectures and runtime auditing [8–10]. The literature therefore motivates a repeatable, traceable benchmark that (a) measures end‑to‑end operational success in emulation, (b) records repair invocation counts and provider audit traces, and (c) preserves deterministic seeds and exclusion rules for exact reproducibility. NetOpsTraceBench implements these desiderata and contributes a fully archived run for follow‑up sensitivity analysis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and scope. The experimental plan was preregistered (rX4f7-1) and froze task selection, inclusion/exclusion thresholds, stopping criteria, seeds, the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), and the analysis plan prior to observing outcomes. The benchmark scope specified 1,200 paired tasks (edge = 600, core = 600), public synthetic or consented examples only, vendor‑agnostic canonical device command sequences, and deterministic contamination detection rules (token/subsequence overlap and optional embedding similarity with conservative thresholds). Inclusion was automatic: pairs flagged for contamination or for which both episodes failed to return parsable vendor renderings after one automated re‑execution were excluded and logged.

Pipelines and orchestration. We compared (A) Baseline one‑shot — a single LLM call producing an initial candidate, and (B) Guarded verifier‑assisted — the same initial candidate plus at most one automated repair iteration when the deterministic validator rejected the candidate. The preregistration limited initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The requested_model was gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) and the orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed parsing, intent‑constraint checks, and emulator preflight. The task generator was deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and all seeds were frozen.

Execution instrumentation and primary metric. The run recorded provider audit events, raw LLM outputs, validator traces, emulator execution logs, repair prompts/traces, and a full artifact hash manifest. The preregistered binary episode success rule required: (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration; (2) emulator execution with no availability degradation above tolerance; and (3) no automatic rollback event during simulated execution. The preregistration originally specified a nonparametric paired Wilcoxon signed‑rank test; because observed outcomes are strictly binary, the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired contingency table and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. This analytic choice and its documentation are archived with the analysis artifacts.

Representative diagnostics and artifact examples. Validator traces for representative tasks show that initial shared candidates frequently satisfied the intent constraints and passed parsing—e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json indicates validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for task-000001. Task manifest entries (e.g., task-000001 required_sequence and intent fields) demonstrate that many synthetic tasks contained explicit, small ordered sequences (shutdown → change → restore) that map directly to short command lists; such task structure reduces ambiguity and therefore reduces repair invocation frequency. The provider audit stage_counts corroborate that low repair frequency (repair = 3) and model_calls_used = 1,203 reflect the execution dynamics under our frozen policy.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation and power considerations. The observed near‑ceiling baseline (≈99.75%) constrained absolute headroom for improvement and therefore the realized power to detect small absolute gains. The preregistered power plan targeted a 5 percentage‑point minimum detectable effect (MDE) at two‑sided α = 0.05 and power 0.8 under assumed baseline ≈0.70; the observed baseline of ≈0.9975 implies the run was underpowered to detect the ≈0.25 percentage‑point gain we observed. The archived bootstrap CI and contingency counts quantify this: with n10 = 3 and n01 = 0, the exact McNemar p = 0.25 and the 95% CI includes zero, consistent with a null result under the preregistered MDE.

Operational explanation for low repair invocation. Two artifact‑grounded factors explain why the guarded pipeline was rarely exercised. First, the synthetic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced tasks with precise required sequences and constrained allowed fields, reducing intent ambiguity (see representative task_manifest entries such as task-000001 and task-000003). Second, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied strict parsing and intent‑constraint checking that, in combination with the generator's constrained patterns, accepted most initial candidates. The joint evidence—task manifests, scoring traces, and provider stage_counts—supports the interpretation that corpus and validator configuration choices materially reduced the opportunity for repair to improve outcomes.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strong: deterministic seeds, preregistered exclusion rules, and automated logging avoid human adjudication bias. Construct validity requires caution: the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) is a conservative operational proxy but may not fully capture nuanced operational risk in production. External validity is limited: only the requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was exercised, tasks were synthetic or consented and vendor‑agnostic, and Mininet‑style emulation may not reflect vendor idiosyncrasies, routing convergence delays, or telemetry noise found in production. Conclusion validity: the very low discordant counts limit inferential sensitivity for small absolute effects. These threats are documented in the preregistration and in the run artifacts.

Implications and recommendations. Under constrained, well‑specified tasks where an LLM initial candidate already satisfies deterministic verifier checks, generate–validate–repair is infrequently invoked and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier utility more decisively, future benchmarks should (a) include intentionally ambiguous or adversarial intents, (b) vary validator strictness to exercise repair pathways, (c) increase sample sizes or select tasks with lower anticipated baseline success to recover power for small effects, and (d) test multiple model families and fine‑tuned variants. The archived artifacts (provider traces, validator logs, task manifests) enable exact reproduction of the current run and straightforward sensitivity studies that modify those axes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs. Under our synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator settings, and gpt-5-mini as requested, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) with exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 and a 95% bootstrap CI that includes zero. Provider audit (model_calls_used = 1,203; repair-stage calls = 3), representative validator traces, and task manifests indicate that conservative task design and validator acceptance largely explain the small measured effect. The run artifacts and analysis code are archived to enable reproducible follow‑up studies that vary corpus difficulty, validator strictness, and model families to identify operational regimes where verifier scaffolding yields meaningful gains.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
